chapter_theme: The herald names the last of the kings to the bride, who gives her heart to a young prince before he is named and garlands him; the rejected kings accept it as karma, the wedding is held and the swayamvara closes; a second swayamvara gives the girl Sutara to Srivijayan, and the poet ends the sarukkam by telling all to remember the fruit of deeds.

1817.reading: The guide points out the lord of the Hemangada land, whose northern wind carries lotus petals, lily pollen and the white flowers of sugarcane to the coral-legged gold mansions.
1817.nuance: The verse is praise of the king's land more than of the king; the man himself is named only by his country.
1817.event: The herald shows the bride the lord of the Hemangada country.

1818.reading: The guide shows the lord of Kalinga and the young king of Magadha, who sits on a lion throne and owns hills of gem-bright streams.
1818.event: The herald shows the bride the lord of Kalinga and the king of Magadha.

1819.reading: The guide names the kings of Anga, Avanti, Kosala (the lily-hued one) and Vanga, praising the Ganga-washed land of the last as she points to the spear-armed youth.
1819.event: The herald shows the bride the lords of Anga, Avanti, Kosala and Vanga.

1820.reading: The bride is led round the moonlit courtyard, her soft feet aching, past many armed kings, and the guide then shows her in detail the Vidyadhara kings who sit on gem couches on the north side of the mansion.
1820.nuance: The verb சொன்னாள் is feminine, whereas chapter 78 casts the herald as a man; the guide is kept as one figure here and the discrepancy is noted in source_issues.
1820.event: The herald walks the bride round the hall and names the earthly kings, then the Vidyadhara kings on the north side.

1821.reading: The guide tells the bride that the Vidyadhara kings, whose qualities she can hear, are no different from the gods save that they blink.
1821.nuance: The praise rests on the old mark of the gods that they do not blink; the herald uses it to say these kings differ from gods only in that one thing.
1821.event: The herald praises the Vidyadhara kings of the silver mountain as godlike.

1822.reading: While the guide still tells of the kings' cities and lines, the bride's large eyes had already settled on the young spear-bearing prince, heir of the king named for the sun.
1822.nuance: The heir is named only by the sun-king's epithet; line 2 is hard to construe, and that the heir is the groom later called the cousin prince (1828) is inferred.
1822.event: The bride's gaze settles on the prince whom the herald has not yet reached.

1823.reading: Her eyes fall on the garland of his chest like a bee drawn by the rut-scent of a great elephant.
1823.event: The bride's eyes fall on the prince of the elephant with the face-cloth.

1824.reading: The guide had only pointed him out, but her restraint and her heart had already gone to him, and the fruit of her enjoyment-lot had ripened, so the herald's words were no use.
1824.nuance: போக பான்மை is read as the portion of enjoyment owed her; the verse does not say it is the fruit of a past deed, so no link rests on that.
1824.event: The bride gives up her restraint at the sight of the prince before the herald has done naming him.

claims.claim: the lot of enjoyment ripens by itself and the herald's introduction adds nothing to it

1825.reading: Her restraint broken, trembling and ashamed, she lets the bee-covered garland fall on the saffron-heaped shoulders of the prince, and the hall roars.
1825.event: The bride puts the garland on the prince's shoulders, choosing him.

1826.reading: Drums, conches and war-drums sound, flowers and golden powder fill the quarters, and the rejected kings sweat and sigh.
1826.nuance: The rejected kings are the same men the herald praised in 1817-1821, now left without comment.
1826.event: The hall erupts in noise and flowers as the rejected kings sweat and sigh.

1827.reading: Their hope gone and their eyes held by the prince's form as by a fetter, the kings calm themselves with the thought that deeds ripen as they will, not as one wishes, and that this is how deeds go.
1827.nuance: The kings' consolation is the same doctrine the poet urges on all in the last verse of the chapter (1839); here it is reported as their thought and not argued.
1827.event: The rejected kings give up their claim by thinking that the outcome is the work of karma.

claims.claim: deeds ripen in their own way and not as one wishes, so a loss is to be borne as the nature of karma

1828.reading: The question is put of what the flaming-discus king did when the soft-speaking girl garlanded the cousin prince from the mountain world, and the answer is that he saw the wedding completed for the spear-bearer.
1828.nuance: Line 1 (நெய்த்தலைப் பாலுக்காங்கு) is obscure, and who the flaming-discus king is, host or kinsman, is not stated.
1828.event: The discus-king completes the wedding rites for the spear-bearing prince.

1829.reading: The spear-bearer spreads out fine ornaments before the kings of the earth, bathes the renowned in splendour and has a rain of gold fall.
1829.nuance: The sense of lines 2-3 (the kings bringing water, being bathed) is uncertain; read as honouring the guests with gifts.
1829.event: Gifts of jewels and gold are poured out to honour the kings who came.

1830.reading: The wedding fire is laid with jewel-bright rice, river sand and darbha, with fuel fit for a great king, and shines richer than any wealth.
1830.nuance: Pure description of the rite's setting; no one acts in the verse.

1831.reading: When the fire sacrifice is done and the bride circles the flame with the youth, the drops of sweat on her ear-ringed face are like nectar dots on the moon.
1831.event: The bride and groom circle the sacred fire.

1832.reading: The prince lies with the girl in the mansion on the aloe-scented couch, while his father Arkkakirti, whose sceptre and spear rule, has the swayamvara brought to its close.
1832.event: The groom consummates the marriage and his father ends the swayamvara.

1833.reading: On the day after the first choosing, kings take seats on gold couches to the sound of drums, a mountain-king tells the girl each one's character and a lotus-eyed woman is shown.
1833.nuance: The verse is hard to parse: whether the lotus-eyed woman is the guide or the bride, and who the mountain-king is, are not said.
1833.event: A second swayamvara is held; the mountain-king describes each king to the girl.

1834.reading: The girl, like a peahen, looks over the kings as a range of hills and longs for the golden peak that is the flaming-discus king's son.
1834.event: The girl's eyes choose the discus-king's son from the assembled kings.

1835.reading: Sutara's garland of flowers and bees falls on the hero's golden chest while the other kings wither, and kin on both sides gladly complete the wedding.
1835.event: Sutara garlands the hero and her kin complete the wedding.

1836.reading: The sea-hued one's son, whose feet wear the warrior's anklet, circles the fire with the bride and after the rite joins her.
1836.event: The groom circles the fire with the bride and is united with her.

1837.reading: Both couples, the lady of gentle grace with the dark-gem lord's son and the lady named for light with the sun's son, delight in love and go to their homes on the great mountain.
1837.nuance: Which bride is which of the two named in lines 1 and 3 is not said; they are read as the two weddings of the chapter.
1837.event: The two newly wedded pairs depart for the mountain land.

1838.reading: Srivijayan, whose command stands against enemy kings' victory, enters the joyous palace of victory with his wife as lovely as Tiru.
1838.nuance: The wording of lines 1-2 plays on the word விசயம் (victory) and is a pun on his name; read as praise.
1838.event: Srivijayan enters his palace with his bride.

1839.reading: The poet closes by saying that such wealth here and the pleasure of the flower-decked gods are the fruit of one's deeds, and bids people of good nature to remember it daily and keep to the way.
1839.nuance: The closing moral sets the kings' resigned thought at 1827 as the poet's own teaching, and prepares the opening of the next sarukkam (1840-1844), where Payapati reasons from his kingship to merit.

claims.claim: great wealth in this world and heavenly enjoyment are the fruit of deeds, and people should remember this and keep to the right way

links.note: 1824 says the herald's showing was needless because her lot of enjoyment had already ripened; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate, which reaches first even when one tries another way.
links.teaches: A choice that looks free and quick is shown to have been set before the guide's words, which a bare general rule about fate does not show.

gains.a: The verse gains a general rule that fate comes before any human device, which would otherwise be only an aside about her lot.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene in which a formal, careful introduction is overtaken by fate in a glance.

links.note: 1827 has kings with every means to win her calm themselves because deeds ripen as they will; Kural 377 says even those who have gathered millions enjoy only what the apportioner has apportioned.
links.teaches: Fate's apportioning is shown over a bride and not over wealth, among men whose rank and army were equal, so the rule is tested where effort was all in place.

gains.a: The kings' calm gains a stated general law behind it, which the verse leaves as their passing thought.
gains.b: The couplet gains a contest in which every competitor had equal means, the case where apportioning alone must decide.

links.note: 1827 shows kings who lose the bride calming themselves by seeing the loss as karma; Naladiyar 33 contrasts the fool who sighs hotly at the fruit of deeds with the wise who call it old desert.
links.teaches: The same step from sighing to calm is shown as a group's act on a public loss, where the quatrain gives only the principle.

gains.a: The kings' calm gains a named opposite, the fool who sighs and breaks, which the scene alone does not give.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case of powerful men who choose the wise answer after having sweated and sighed, as 1826 shows.

links.note: 1839 states for everyone the thought that 1827 reports of the rejected kings: the fruit of deeds is what comes.
links.teaches: The kings' private resignation is the lesson the poet then gives to all readers, so the swayamvara scene is built to carry it.

links.note: 1839 bids all remember the fruit of deeds; 1842 shows Payapati reasoning that the pleasure of his grandchildren is the fruit of swollen merit with more seed to sow.
links.teaches: The poet's general advice becomes a king's own reasoning, which turns the closing moral of one sarukkam into the opening act of the next.

links.note: 1839 says wealth and heavenly pleasure are the fruit of deeds and bids remembering; Tirumanthiram 267 says joy and sorrow were fixed by earlier acts and that fools who see joy yet do not give know no virtue.
links.teaches: The poem asks only for remembering the fruit and keeping to the way; the couplet names what that way includes, giving, and what its absence shows.

gains.a: The poet's advice to keep to the way gains one concrete act, giving, as the proof that the fruit has been understood.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a story of fruit at its fullest, a royal wedding and gods' pleasure, set against which its warning to the unmoved has its force.

cast.role: the guide who names the kings to the bride (a man in chapter 78; here the verb சொன்னாள் is feminine)
the king's daughter shown the kings and who garlands the prince; not named in this chapter's verses
the rejected kings of the swayamvara
the flaming-discus king who sees a wedding completed and whose son the second bride chooses; probably Tivittan, not named
the groom's father of the first wedding, named at 1832; at 1829 the unnamed spear-bearer is taken to be him
the prince the first bride garlands; probably Amitatejas of chapter 77, not named here
the mountain-king who describes the kings to the girl at the second swayamvara
the bride of the second swayamvara, named at 1835
the groom of the second wedding, the sea-hued one's son, named at 1838
the hearers the poet addresses at the close

source_issues: 1817-1837 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
Chapter 78 casts the herald as a man (நின்றான்); 1820 line 4 uses the feminine சொன்னாள், so the guide may be a woman; one id is kept.

The bride of the first choosing is never named in these verses (chapter 78 names her Sayambavai); the second bride is named சுதாரை at 1835, and 1837 line 3 names a lady 'of light'. Who is which is not settled by the Tamil here.
1822 line 2 (வெங்கதிரோன் பெயரவனுக்கு ... எனொ) and 1828 line 1 (நெய்த்தலைப் பாலுக்காங்கு) are hard to construe.
